The time required to fold a folding bike varies depending on the specific model. The Cog & Chain Pocket 20 folds in about 12 seconds [1]. For the Larkspur Fold 20, it takes approximately 15 seconds to fold [2]. Some owners of these bikes may find it takes them a little more practice to learn the folding sequence; for the Cog & Chain Pocket 20, most owners master it in under 20 seconds after a couple of days [1].

These bikes are designed for various commuting needs, and with practice, folding them can become quick and intuitive [2]. While some suggest most folding bikes fold in under a minute [3], the specific models mentioned offer relatively quick folding times [1][2].

The ideal weight for a kids' bike depends on the model and intended rider, but lighter bikes are generally easier for children to manage [5]. For young riders, many models are available in 16-inch sizes, which suit most children aged four to six [3][5]. These smaller bikes can be quite light, with models weighing as little as 6.3 kg [3]. A Larkspur Sprout 16, another option, has a weight of 7.2 kg [1].

When selecting a bike, it is important that the rider can comfortably reach the ground with both feet flat when stopped [1]. The Cog & Chain Cub 16, for example, is designed for riders between 98 and 117 cm tall [3]. While the specific weight of a kids' bike is important, the fit and adjustability of the bike are also crucial, as some models feature adjustable seat heights [1][3].

For winter riding, the specific tire pressure depends on your body weight and the type of riding surface you encounter [3]. The pressure range printed on the sidewall serves as a safe guideline, not a fixed target pressure [3]. If you ride on ice regularly, studded tires may be necessary for grip, as normal tires are insufficient on black ice or packed snow [4].

Generally, a slightly softer tire absorbs bumps on real roads, allowing for faster rolling than a very hard tire [1][3]. If your bike feels harsh, bounces over bumps, or loses grip in corners, your pressure is likely too high [1][3]. Conversely, if the ride feels sluggish or squirms, the pressure may be too low, risking pinch flats [3]. For instance, a 75 kg rider on 32 mm tires might use 55 psi front and 60 psi rear [3]. When riding on rough surfaces, lower pressure provided a faster ride compared to higher pressure configurations [1].

Regardless of the season, it is crucial to check your tire pressure weekly because tubes lose air through the rubber, which can equate to 5 to 10 psi in a week without a puncture [1][3]. Furthermore, if you are carrying extra weight, like a loaded pannier, you should increase the pressure accordingly [3].

For commutes exceeding 15 km, a gravel bike setup is often the superior and more comfortable option compared to a flat-bar hybrid [1]. The Larkspur Gravel GX, for instance, is designed for long commutes, dirt roads, and loaded day trips, offering a geometry that is more relaxed than a road race bike but lower and more efficient than a hybrid for headwinds [1]. This gravel bike is suited for mixed commutes involving both roads and paths [1].

The drop bars on the gravel bike provide multiple hand positions and a lower, more efficient riding posture [1]. Conversely, a flat-bar hybrid offers a more upright position, which some riders prefer for short city trips where visibility of traffic is paramount [1]. The Gravel GX, priced at $1,399, is equipped with mounts for fenders, a rear rack, and bottle mounts, making it a capable year-round commuter [1]. For riders seeking a bike for commutes up to 20 km, the Cog & Chain Transit 8 is also available, which is designed for city riding and has features like fenders and a rack [4].

For daily commuting, lubing the chain is recommended every 150 to 300 km, or after riding in heavy rain [1, 2]. If the chain squeaks after a wet ride, it likely needs lubrication that same day to prevent rust on the rollers [1]. A quick wipe-down with a rag is part of the routine, but if the chain is black and gritty, it requires degreasing with a bike-specific cleaner, followed by rinsing and drying [1].

A full cleaning of the chain, which involves degreasing and thorough washing, should be performed about once per month [1]. Some riders find they need to clean and lube every 200 km or so, or after any ride in heavy rain [2]. For riders in salty conditions, like winter riding, it is advised to rinse the drivetrain after each salty ride and lube the chain at least twice a week [4]. Additionally, a full cleaning process, such as a detailed maintenance session, might be suggested every other weekend for some commuters [3].

Truing a wheel yourself is possible, often requiring a spoke key and taking time to learn the nuances [1][2]. A wheel wobbling side to side indicates it is out of true, which can happen after hitting a pothole or curb [1][3]. Before attempting a repair, verify that the wheel is properly seated in the dropouts and the axle is tight, as a loose wheel might mimic being out of true [3]. If you decide to repair it yourself, you can use a cable tie to check the wobble while testing the adjustments [1].

When making adjustments, you must work slowly; large turns can introduce new issues [2]. To move the rim away from the rub, you should loosen spokes on one side by a quarter turn and tighten spokes on the opposite side by a quarter turn, focusing on the side causing the rub [1][2][3]. However, if the rim is dented, cracked, or if spokes are broken, professional help is needed [2][3]. If you are unsure or the damage is significant, a shop visit may be worth the cost, which ranges from $25 to $40 depending on the service and replacements [1][2][3].

The Cog & Chain Transit 8 is a commuter bicycle available with a five-year frame warranty [1]. This model is an 8-speed aluminum city bike equipped with fenders, a rack, and mechanical disc brakes [1]. It is designed to be a light, ready-to-ride city bike suitable for commutes ranging from 5 to 20 km [1]. The bike weighs 12.6 kg and is priced at $799 [1].

The Transit 8 features an aluminum frame and a steel fork, paired with an 8-speed derailleur and an 11-34 cassette [1]. This setup allows for low gears, making it well-suited for riders tackling steep hills in urban environments [1]. Its components include 700 x 38c tires, which perform well on pavement yet remain capable on broken asphalt and gravel paths [1]. The frame accommodates the rack and fenders via threaded mounts, preventing rattling on uneven surfaces [1].

Several factors can contribute to reducing flats on a commuter bike. One preventative measure is ensuring your tires are in good condition, as common causes for flats include low pressure, a thorn or wire still embedded in the tire, or simply worn tires [1]. Furthermore, if you are concerned about flats, switching to tubeless tires may be beneficial, as they can seal many small punctures on their own, which is helpful for commuters who ride through glass [1].

Regarding proper setup, the pressure you run in your tires matters significantly for a comfortable and efficient ride. While some riders initially inflate to the maximum sidewall pressure, finding a lower pressure that feels calm over bumps is often better for comfort, even when carrying a full pannier [4]. For instance, riders found that running lower pressures allows the bike to absorb bumps rather than bouncing over them, which is critical on rough roads [3]. Advanced options, like the Larkspur Gravel GX, are available with tubeless-ready tires and wider options for various commutes [2].

For riders encountering overheating on steep inclines, the type of motor and riding technique matters greatly [1][3]. The Larkspur Haul, an electric longtail cargo bike, advises that when tackling a steep hill with a full load, riders should shift down early to a low gear and utilize the highest assist level [1]. Maintaining a high cadence helps keep the motor in its strongest range, which assists in preventing overheating [1].

In contrast, the Cog & Chain Current E, which has a mid-drive motor, is designed for riders with real hills on their commute [3]. Because this mid-drive motor drives through the bike's gears, it can remain in its efficient speed range while climbing a steep climb instead of bogging down [3]. The Larkspur Volt E1, which uses a rear hub motor, is suited for mixed terrain but a mid-drive motor is generally better for efficiently climbing steep hills [2].

If you are experiencing repeated flats, there are several common causes to investigate [1][3]. One major issue is that the tire may still contain the object that caused the initial puncture, such as a thorn or glass shard [1][3]. Furthermore, riding with insufficiently inflated tires can lead to pinch flats, where the tube is crushed between the tire and the rim [1][3]. Other potential causes include worn tires with thin tread or a slipped rim tape exposing a spoke hole [1].

To prevent future flats, riders should inspect the inside of the tire carefully before installing a new tube to ensure all debris is removed [1][2]. Additionally, maintaining proper tire pressure and replacing worn tires are crucial maintenance steps [1]. A good repair kit should include a spare tube, tire levers, a patch kit, and a pump or CO2 inflator [1][3]. If you are getting flats frequently, you might also want to check your original causes, which could include low pressure or worn components [3].
